question_text: What is the essential difference between the larvae and adults of echinoderms, symmetry wise?

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The larva
steps.why: The larva keeps the older symmetry of the group, so it is the larva and not the adult that shows where echinoderms belong in classification.
common_mistakes: Writing that the larva is radial. Only the adult is radial.
Writing that the larva is fixed to the bottom. The larva swims freely.
steps.memory_tip: Swimming larva is bilateral; settled adult is radial.
steps.margin_note: One line for the symmetry and one for the habit.

steps.label: The adult
steps.why: The adult settles on the sea bottom, where food can arrive from any direction, and a body built on five parts round an axis suits that position.
common_mistakes: Writing radial alone. The adult symmetry is pentamerous radial symmetry.
Writing that both stages have the same symmetry. The change of symmetry is the whole point of the question.
steps.memory_tip: Bilateral first, radial second — the five-part radial form comes later.
steps.margin_note: The boxed contrast is the answer. Add the word pentamerous, it carries the mark.
